title: Best Time to Seal Asphalt Driveway: Late Spring to Fall
h1: Best Time of Year to Seal an Asphalt Driveway

description: The best time of year to seal an asphalt driveway is late spring to early fall, on 2-3 dry days above 50°F. Early fall is often the safest window.
dek: The best time of year to seal an asphalt driveway is late spring to early fall, on 2-3 dry days above 50°F.
intro: The best time of year to seal an asphalt driveway is late spring through early fall, and early fall is often the most dependable window: warm days, lower humidity, fewer storms, and a fresh coat going into winter. Within that season, pick a run of two or three dry days with air and pavement at 50°F or warmer day and night, and start mid-morning once the dew is gone.

There is no single best month for everyone. A homeowner in Minnesota has a short window from about late May to mid-September, while one in Georgia can seal most of the year but should dodge the muggy, stormy midsummer. This guide gives the window by region, the case for each season, how late in the year you can push it, and the best time of day to start.
quickAnswer: Seal between late spring and early fall, on a stretch of 2 to 3 dry days when air and pavement stay at 50°F or above, including overnight. In the North, late August to mid-September is the sweet spot; in the South and desert Southwest, spring and fall beat midsummer; in the Pacific Northwest, July to early September. Start mid-morning, never at night.

blocks.p: Across all regions, the conditions matter more than the date. Most water-based asphalt sealer labels ask for air and pavement at 50°F or more and rising during application and for a period afterward, a dry surface, and no rain for at least 24 hours. The season is just where those conditions line up most reliably.

Two questions come before choosing a season. Is the driveway old enough? New asphalt needs six to twelve months first, covered in [when to seal a new asphalt driveway](/when-should-you-seal-a-new-asphalt-driveway/). And does it need sealing this year at all? If water still beads on the surface, the right time may be next year; [how often should you seal your driveway](/how-often-should-you-seal-your-driveway/) explains the check.

sections.h: What Time of Year Should You Seal an Asphalt Driveway?

blocks.p: Late spring, summer and early fall all work. Each has one big advantage and one big risk.

head: Season
Main advantage
Main risk
rows: Protects before summer UV; fixes cracks winter opened
Cold nights and heavy dew if left too late
Cold, dew and frost stop curing

blocks.p: Sealing in late spring sets the driveway up for the strongest sun of the year and lets you fill the cracks winter opened. The catch is unsettled weather and pavement that is still damp from a wet spring. Wait until nights have reliably warmed and the ground has dried, rather than jumping at the first warm weekend in April.

Summer has the warmest, steadiest drying weather in most of the country, so coats cure fast. The risks are very hot pavement and afternoon thunderstorms. In hot regions, morning starts beat midday in July and August.

For many climates this is the best season. Days are still warm, humidity often drops, storms are less frequent, and the new coat goes into winter keeping freeze-thaw water out of the surface. The only danger is waiting too long.

sections.h: What Is the Best Month to Seal a Driveway Where You Live?

blocks.p: The upper Midwest, Great Lakes, New England and mountain areas have the shortest season, roughly late May into mid-September. Late August and early September are often the sweet spot: warm days, nights that are cooler but still above the label minimum, and less rain than late spring. After mid-September the margin shrinks fast.
The window runs from about May into early October. Summer humidity slows drying, so drier spells in late spring and early fall usually give the best results. Plan around pop-up summer thunderstorms.
You can seal for much of the year, but summer brings high humidity and almost daily afternoon storms. Spring and fall are usually better, with lower humidity and steadier weather.
Summer pavement gets extremely hot, which can make sealer skin over before it bonds. Spring and fall are the better seasons; in summer, an early-morning start is close to mandatory.

Summers are dry and the rest of the year is wet, so July through early September is typically best, before fall rains arrive. Coastal fog and marine air slow drying even in summer, so pick sunny days with a dry forecast for the following day too.

sections.h: What Weather Do You Need to Seal a Driveway?

blocks.p: Warm, dry and stable: air and pavement at 50°F or above and rising, a fully dry surface, low to moderate humidity, and at least 24 hours without rain afterward. Some products set a higher minimum or a longer rain-free period, so check your pail.

The air temperature while you work, the pavement temperature (shaded asphalt on a cool morning can be colder than the air, and sunny asphalt far hotter), and the overnight low after each coat. All three need to clear the label minimum. Detailed temperature rules, including how to measure pavement with an infrared thermometer, are in [minimum temperature for sealing a driveway](/what-temperature-to-seal-driveway/).

After rain or washing, give the pavement at least 24 hours of dry weather, longer in shaded or low areas. Press a paper towel into a dark-looking spot; if it picks up moisture, wait. Sealer over damp asphalt is a leading cause of peeling within the first year.

Humid air slows evaporation, so a sticky 88°F day can dry slower than a crisp 68°F one. When you can choose between hot and humid or mild and dry, mild and dry usually gives the better coat. Clear nights after warm days in late summer and fall produce heavy dew that can cloud a coat that has not set.
Read the hourly forecast for the day you seal and the next 24 to 48 hours, not the daily icon. If rain does catch you, [rain after driveway sealing](/rain-after-driveway-sealing/) covers what to do.

sections.h: How Late in the Year Can You Seal a Driveway?

blocks.p: As late as both daytime and overnight temperatures stay at or above the label minimum, usually 50°F, for at least a day or two after sealing. In northern states that usually means finishing by mid-September; in milder regions, October can still work.

blocks.h3: Is it OK to seal blacktop in October?

blocks.p: In the mid-Atlantic, the central states and the South, often yes, on a warm, dry spell where nights stay above 50°F. In the North, October nights regularly fall into the 30s and 40s, and short days with heavy dew leave a coat little time to cure. A coat that does not cure before the first freeze can peel by spring.

blocks.h3: A warm day with a cold night

blocks.p: A common question: what if the day reaches the mid-70s but the night falls to the upper 30s? That is not a good sealing day. The coat keeps curing for many hours after it is dry to the touch, and a night well below 50°F stalls it. The label minimum applies overnight too, so wait for a window where the low stays at or above it.

Wait until spring. One more winter on an unsealed driveway does far less harm than a coat that never cures. Use the off-season to fill cracks on any mild, dry day the filler label allows, and buy the sealer once the weather turns.

sections.h: Can You Seal a Driveway in Very Hot Weather?

blocks.p: Yes, with care. Summer gives the fastest curing in most regions, and sun helps. The problem is extreme pavement heat: black asphalt in full midsummer sun can run far above the air temperature, and sealer on a very hot surface can skin over on top before it bonds underneath.

Some labels set an upper temperature limit; others suggest lightly misting the pavement with water just before applying, with no standing puddles. Whatever brand you use, check its stated maximum and follow it. Popular premium sealers and budget pails alike can flash dry on very hot asphalt.

blocks.h3: How to work in summer heat

ul: Start as soon as the dew is gone and the surface is dry.
Finish before the pavement reaches peak heat in early afternoon.
In hot regions, late-afternoon application can work if the overnight low stays well above the label minimum and there is no dew or rain risk.
Mist the surface lightly ahead of the squeegee if the label allows it.

blocks.p: In many areas, the bigger summer risk is the afternoon thunderstorm, not the heat. Morning starts help with both. Product picks that list fast-dry or heat-tolerant formulas are in the [best asphalt driveway sealer](/best-asphalt-driveway-sealer-reviews/) list.

sections.h: What Time of Day Is Best to Seal a Driveway?

blocks.p: Mid-morning, once the dew has evaporated and the pavement is warming. That gives each coat most of the day to set before temperatures fall and evening moisture arrives.
Early-morning pavement is often damp with dew and still cold from the night. Sealer over dew-damp asphalt bonds poorly and can look mottled.

A coat started after mid-afternoon faces falling temperatures and evening dew before it has dried. Drying stalls overnight and the finish can turn cloudy or stay tacky into the next day. It also leaves no time for a second coat the same day.

blocks.h3: Can you seal a driveway at night?

blocks.p: No. Temperatures drop after sunset, dew forms, and the coat gets no sun to drive off its water. Even in a hot climate where night temperatures stay high, you lose the light you need to see thin spots and puddles. Seal in daylight and give the coat the warm hours.
If you can arrange it, a weekday morning has advantages: fewer neighbors running sprinklers or washing cars, lighter traffic, and less demand for contractors and supplies.

sections.h: When Is the Best Time to Repair and Seal a Driveway?

blocks.p: Do the repairs a day or more before you seal, in the same dry, warm window. Crack filler and cold patch need time to set before sealer goes over them, and they need the same conditions the sealer does.

head: Day
Task
rows: Trim edges, clean, degrease, fill cracks and patch holes
Two thin coats of sealer, starting mid-morning
Keep cars off while it cures

blocks.h3: Fill cracks even when you are not sealing

blocks.p: Crack filling protects the base, which is what actually decides how long the driveway lasts. Fill cracks wider than about 1/8 inch each spring or fall when they appear, even in years when the surface does not need a coat. Products by crack width are in [best driveway crack filler](/best-driveway-crack-filler/).

blocks.h3: Line it up with other work

blocks.p: If the driveway needs patching by a paving contractor, schedule that first and seal afterward, following the contractor's advice on how long fresh patches should cure. If you plan to hire a sealcoating crew, book early in the season; good crews fill their calendars, and [how much does it cost to seal a driveway](/how-much-does-it-cost-to-seal-a-driveway/) explains what a fair quote includes. The step-by-step DIY method is in [how to seal a driveway](/how-to-seal-a-driveway/).

sections.h: How Do You Plan the Weekend You Seal?

blocks.p: Plan around a weather window of three days: one for prep, one for coating, and one for the first night and day of curing.

Look at the hourly forecast for all three days, including overnight lows and the chance of evening storms. A 30 percent chance of a 6 p.m. thunderstorm on the day of the second coat is a real risk. Turn off sprinklers that reach the driveway a day before and keep them off for a day after.

When the forecast is marginal on temperature, rain or humidity, wait a week. A delayed seal costs nothing. A coat applied in borderline weather can peel, stay soft or wash away, and fixing it means scraping and redoing the work.

If storms show on radar before you start, do not start; sealer in the pail keeps. If rain shows up partway through, finish the section you are on to a straight line, stop, and rinse your tools. Resume once the surface has dried completely, overlapping the old edge only slightly. If temperatures drop unexpectedly overnight, keep cars off longer and check the coat with a fingernail before driving on it; [how long driveway sealer takes to dry](/how-long-for-driveway-sealer-to-dry/) covers how to judge it.

mistakes: The air can read 55°F while shaded pavement is still in the 40s after a cold night, and sealer reacts to the surface it is on. Check the pavement with an infrared thermometer, especially in shade, and confirm the overnight low stays above the label minimum too.

Late-fall days can feel pleasant, but short days, cold nights and heavy dew slow curing badly. A coat that does not cure before the first freeze can peel by spring. In the North, finish by about mid-September; elsewhere, aim for early fall rather than late.

A sun icon says nothing about a 6 p.m. thunderstorm or overnight showers. Read the hourly forecast for sealing day and the 24 to 48 hours after it. If there is a meaningful chance of rain anywhere in that window, move the job to the next good stretch.

Asphalt can look dry an hour after rain while moisture still sits in pores, cracks and shaded edges. Sealer laid over that moisture will not bond well. Give the driveway at least a full day of dry weather and test damp-looking spots with a paper towel before you start.

An afternoon start leaves each coat little time before temperatures fall and dew forms, which slows drying and can cloud the finish, and it rules out a same-day second coat. Start mid-morning once the dew is gone, or earlier in very hot weather.
bottomLine: The best time of year to seal an asphalt driveway is whenever warm, dry, stable weather lines up for two or three days in a row, and in most regions that means late spring through early fall, with early fall often the safest bet. Choose the window for your region, read the hourly forecast instead of the daily icon, make sure the overnight low clears 50°F, start mid-morning after the dew, and postpone without regret when conditions are marginal. A well-timed coat bonds properly and lasts its full two to three years; a rushed late-season one can need redoing by spring.

faqs.q: What is the best time of year to seal an asphalt driveway?
faqs.a: Late spring through early fall in most of the US, on a stretch of two or three dry days with air and pavement at 50°F or above day and night. Early fall is often the most dependable: still warm, usually drier and less stormy, and it protects the surface before winter freeze-thaw cycles begin.

faqs.q: Is it better to seal a driveway in spring or fall?
faqs.a: Both work. Spring sealing prepares the driveway for summer sun and fixes winter cracks, but spring weather is often wet and cool. Early fall usually brings steadier, drier weather and protects the surface heading into winter. With fall, the key is not leaving it too late, when cold nights and dew slow curing.

faqs.q: Is it OK to seal blacktop in October?
faqs.a: In milder regions, often yes, if both days and nights stay at or above the label minimum, usually 50°F, for a day or two after sealing. In northern states, October nights often drop into the 30s and 40s, so the coat may not cure before frost. There, finish by mid-September and otherwise wait for spring.

faqs.q: Can you seal a driveway at night?
faqs.a: No. Temperatures fall after dark, dew forms on the pavement, and there is no sun to drive water out of the coat, so it stays soft and can cloud. You also cannot see thin spots and puddles well. Start mid-morning so each coat gets the warmest hours of the day.

faqs.q: What time of day is best to seal a driveway?
faqs.a: Mid-morning, once the dew has burned off and the pavement is warming. That gives each coat most of the day to dry before temperatures drop and evening dew forms. Starting at dawn risks damp pavement; starting late in the afternoon leaves the coat to face cooling and moisture before it sets.

faqs.q: Can you seal a driveway in summer heat?
faqs.a: Yes. Summer offers the fastest curing in most regions. The concerns are very hot pavement, which can make sealer skin over before it bonds, and afternoon storms. In hot climates, start early in the morning, mist the surface lightly if the label allows, and check the label for a maximum temperature.

faqs.q: How long after rain can I seal my driveway?
faqs.a: Wait at least a full day of dry weather after rain, and longer if the driveway is shaded or has low spots that hold water. The surface must be dry, not just dry-looking. Press a paper towel into darker areas to check. Sealer applied over trapped moisture often peels within the first year.
